name: California

laws.title: Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (TFAIA)
laws.bill: SB 53 · Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act
laws.description: Requires covered large frontier developers to publish safety frameworks and disclose assessments. Includes critical incident reporting and employee whistleblower protections.
laws.timing: Signed 29 September 2025; general effective date 1 January 2026. Some provisions have separate timing or funding conditions.
laws.limits: Frontier-developer and large-developer definitions determine scope; this is not a general obligation on every AI startup. CalCompute provisions depend on an appropriation. The Department of Technology’s first definition-review recommendations are due by 1 January 2027.

laws.title: Training data transparency
laws.description: Requires developers of covered generative AI services made available to Californians to publish a high-level summary of their training datasets, with specified information about sources, licensing, and personal data.
laws.timing: Disclosure deadline: 1 January 2026; applies to covered releases from 1 January 2022.

laws.title: Companion chatbot safeguards
laws.bill: SB 243 · Business & Professions Code § 22601 et seq.
laws.description: Requires human-versus-AI disclosures in specified circumstances, safeguards for known minors, and protocols addressing suicide and self-harm content. Provides a civil remedy for qualifying injuries.
laws.timing: Enacted 13 October 2025; annual reporting begins 1 July 2027.

laws.title: AI in health coverage review
laws.description: Sets conditions for AI, algorithms, and software used in utilization review. Requires individualized clinical information and equitable application, while preserving qualified human review of medical-necessity decisions.
laws.timing: Enacted 28 September 2024; consult the amended code for operative requirements.

laws.title: Online bot identity disclosures
laws.description: Prohibits using a bot to mislead a person in California about its artificial identity for specified commercial or election-deception purposes.
laws.timing: Operative since 1 July 2019.
laws.appliesTo: Persons using covered automated online accounts to communicate or interact with people in California.
obligations: A clear, conspicuous disclosure that the account is a bot avoids liability under this section.
laws.limits: The specified deceptive intent and commercial or election purpose are required. The chapter does not impose a duty on online-platform service providers.

summary: Selected laws covering frontier model safety, training data, companion chatbots, and health coverage decisions.

name: Colorado

laws.title: Automated decision-making protections
laws.bill: SB 26-189 · Replaces the earlier Colorado AI Act
laws.description: Sets documentation, consumer notice, recordkeeping, data-correction, and human-review duties for covered automated systems used in consequential decisions. Enforced by the attorney general.
laws.timing: Signed 14 May 2026; key duties start 1 January 2027. Draft implementing rules were filed 11 August 2026.
laws.limits: This is the replacement framework, not the original SB 24-205 obligations. Proposed implementing rules are still in rulemaking as of this review. Follow the attorney general’s current notices for changes.

summary: A revised framework for consequential automated decisions, with key duties starting in 2027.

name: Texas

laws.title: Responsible AI Governance Act
laws.description: Prohibits specified harmful and intentionally discriminatory AI uses. Includes disclosures for government and certain health-care interactions, attorney-general enforcement, and a regulatory sandbox. Coverage and exemptions depend on the activity.
laws.timing: Effective 1 January 2026.

summary: A statewide framework targeting specific AI harms, disclosures, and government oversight.

name: Utah

laws.title: Generative AI consumer disclosures
laws.description: Requires disclosures for certain generative AI interactions in consumer transactions and regulated services. Establishes responsibility for consumer-protection violations involving AI, with a limited disclosure safe harbor.
laws.timing: Enacted in 2025; consult the amended text for scope and timing.

laws.title: Mental-health chatbot protections
laws.description: Mental-health chatbot suppliers face limits on sharing sensitive information, personalized advertising, and presenting their tools as human.
laws.timing: Effective 7 May 2025.
laws.appliesTo: Suppliers of covered mental-health chatbots used by individuals located in Utah.
obligations: Restrict sharing of identifiable health information and user input, subject to the act’s exceptions.
Disclose AI identity before access, after a gap of seven days, and when asked; clearly identify ads and relevant commercial relationships.
Do not use user input for specified advertising decisions, subject to limited exceptions.
laws.enforcement: The Division of Consumer Protection enforces the chapter, with fines of up to $2,500 per violation.
laws.limits: Scripted-only tools and tools solely connecting people to human therapists are excluded. Section 58-60-118 separately offers a conditional affirmative defense for specified licensing claims; it does not license AI therapists.

laws.title: AI Learning Laboratory & regulatory mitigation
laws.bill: Utah Code Title 13, Chapter 72 · AI Learning Laboratory
laws.description: A supervised programme permits approved businesses to test specified AI uses under agreements with the AI office and relevant regulator. The agreement identifies the particular regulatory relief and conditions.
laws.timing: Existing programme; current scope and authorised pilot register checked 5 October 2026. Pilot dates and status vary.
laws.appliesTo: Businesses accepted into the AI Learning Laboratory with a written regulatory mitigation agreement.
obligations: Follow the agreement’s scope, safeguards, disclosures, reporting, and time limits. Other applicable requirements continue to apply.
laws.limits: Admission is not state endorsement or general product approval. Master agreements alone do not authorise individual pilots. Check the signed agreement and current status for each project.

sources.label: Office of AI Policy · sandbox requirements and statutory links
Official register · agreements and pilot status

summary: Consumer AI disclosures, mental-health chatbot protections, and a supervised AI sandbox with project-specific regulatory relief.

name: New York

laws.title: RAISE Act — amended frontier-model framework
laws.bill: General Business Law Article 44-B · §§1420–1429 · RAISE Act
laws.description: The amended law creates tiered transparency and safety duties for frontier developers, with additional obligations for large developers. The March 2026 amendment replaced the original framework.
laws.timing: Adopted framework; substantive duties take effect 1 January 2027, as stated in the codified sections.
laws.appliesTo: Frontier developers training covered foundation models above 10^26 operations, counting specified later modifications. The model must be developed, deployed or operating wholly or partly in New York. Additional large-developer duties use combined prior-year revenue above $500 million, including affiliates.
obligations: Publish a transparency report before or at deployment of a new or substantially modified frontier model. Covered reports identify the release, uses, supported outputs and contact mechanism; large developers add risk-assessment information.
Large developers must publish and follow a frontier AI framework, review it at least annually, and publish material framework changes with reasons within 30 days.
Report a critical safety incident within 72 hours of the statutory knowledge trigger; disclose imminent death or serious-injury risks to an appropriate authority within 24 hours.
Large developers also submit internal-use risk summaries and maintain the required DFS disclosure statement and assessments.
laws.enforcement: The attorney general can seek up to $1 million for a first covered large-developer violation and $3 million for subsequent violations. The act creates no private right of action.
laws.limits: Academic research by accredited New York colleges/universities and specified Empire AI bodies are excluded. API use alone does not establish frontier-developer status. Catastrophic-risk and incident definitions are narrower than ordinary errors; evaluate modifications and the New York nexus separately.

codeSections.detail: Safety frameworks, public reports and misleading statements.
New York nexus and research exclusions.
Large-developer disclosure filings and DFS assessments.

practicalSteps: Record training compute, affiliate revenue and where the model is developed or offered before classifying coverage.
Assign owners for model releases, public disclosures and urgent incident escalation before the operative date.

laws.title: AI companion safeguards & identity notices
laws.description: Covered AI companions must have self-harm response protocols and tell users they are not talking to a human.
laws.timing: In effect since 5 November 2025. These Article 47 duties are separate from the later Article 48 restrictions for minors.
laws.appliesTo: Operators providing an AI companion for personal use within New York. Section 1700(4) describes systems designed for sustained relationships through retained interaction history, unsolicited emotional questions and ongoing personal dialogue.
obligations: Include a protocol making reasonable efforts to detect and address expressions of suicidal ideation or self-harm, including referral to appropriate crisis services.
Give a conspicuous non-human identity notice at the beginning of interaction (not required more than once daily) and at least every three hours of continued interaction.
laws.enforcement: The attorney general may seek injunctions and civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for violations.
laws.limits: Article 47 excludes specified customer-service-only, research/technical-assistance, efficiency and internal-productivity systems. Its definition is not interchangeable with the broader covered-system definition in the newly enacted Article 48.

codeSections.detail: Companion, operator and New York personal-use definitions.
Attorney general injunctions and daily penalties.

practicalSteps: Test long sessions and returning users to check notice timing and crisis-response routing.
Document the actual product behavior supporting any claimed exclusion; separately assess the minors law.

laws.title: Automated hiring tools in New York City
laws.description: Covered hiring and promotion tools require an independent bias audit, published results, and advance notices. The law is specific to New York City.
laws.timing: DCWP enforcement began 5 July 2023; notices are due 10 business days before use.

sources.label: DCWP law, complaint route & official links

laws.appliesTo: Employers and employment agencies using a covered automated employment decision tool for hiring or promotion in NYC. DCWP includes roles located in NYC at least part-time, remote roles associated with an NYC office, and NYC employment agencies. The tool must substantially assist or replace discretionary decisions under the statutory and rule definitions.
obligations: Before use, ensure an independent bias audit was conducted within the preceding year; follow the required selection/scoring and impact-ratio calculations.
Publish the audit summary and distribution date before use. Keep the required information published for at least six months after the tool’s latest use.

Give NYC-resident candidates and employees the required notice at least 10 business days before use, including assessed qualifications and instructions for requesting an alternative process or reasonable accommodation where available.
laws.enforcement: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) receives complaints and enforces the law.
laws.limits: Not every hiring tool is an AEDT. The rule covers sole reliance on an output, weighting it above every other criterion, or using it to overrule other conclusions. Outreach to people who have not applied for a specific role is distinct. This rule does not itself require an alternative selection process; other accommodation and discrimination duties still apply.

codeSections.detail: Technical scope, substantial assistance and independent-auditor definitions.
Audit calculations, use of historical/test data and public results.
Notice methods, timing and alternative-process/accommodation instructions.

practicalSteps: Map how each score or ranking affects a hiring decision before deciding whether the rule applies.
Ask the vendor for the exact audited version, audit date, data basis and public summary; set a renewal reminder.
If applying for a job, save the notice and published audit and use the employer’s stated accommodation route. Missing audit or notice requirements can be reported to DCWP.

laws.title: Customer biometric information in NYC
laws.bill: NYC Local Law 3 of 2021 · Administrative Code §§22-1201–1205
laws.description: Covered establishments must disclose customer biometric collection and handling. The law also restricts selling or otherwise profiting from biometric-information transactions.
laws.timing: Operative 9 July 2021; separate signage rules prescribe the notice format.
laws.appliesTo: NYC retail stores, food and drink establishments, and entertainment venues handling customer biometric identifiers, such as face geometry or voiceprints.
obligations: Post the prescribed, conspicuous notice at customer entrances when collecting, retaining, converting, storing, or sharing covered information.
Do not sell, lease, trade, share for value, or otherwise profit from transactions in biometric identifier information.
laws.enforcement: Private civil claims: $500 for notice violations or negligent monetization violations; $5,000 for intentional or reckless monetization violations. Notice claims generally require a 30-day cure opportunity; monetization claims do not.
laws.limits: Government collection is excluded. Financial institutions and qualifying non-identification photos or video have notice exceptions. This is not a blanket facial-recognition ban.

laws.title: Tenant data privacy & smart access in NYC
laws.bill: NYC Local Law 63 of 2021 · Administrative Code §§26-3001–3007
laws.description: Residential smart-access systems, including biometric entry, face consent, data-minimization, retention, privacy-policy, and security requirements.
laws.timing: 2021 enactment; the transition for existing smart-access buildings ended 1 January 2023.
laws.appliesTo: Owners of NYC class A multiple dwellings using smart-access systems and covered service providers. HPD identifies biometric entry, key fobs, apps, and other digital access systems.
obligations: Obtain express user consent for reference-data collection and collect only permitted, necessary data.
Provide tenants with a written retention and privacy policy; implement required security safeguards.
Observe 90-day authentication-data destruction or anonymization rules and the separate reference-data deadlines, subject to exceptions.
Do not use access data to harass or evict tenants, or require smart access to enter their own dwelling unit.
laws.enforcement: Section 26-3006 allows occupant claims for unlawful data sales, with compensatory/potential punitive damages or elected damages of $200–$1,000 per sale, plus fees and costs.
laws.limits: This is an access-data law, not a general ban on AI in housing. The specified private action concerns unlawful sales; statutory retention and disclosure exceptions apply.

laws.title: NYC Human Rights Law — discrimination safeguards
laws.description: A separate city discrimination framework relevant to automated decisions in employment, housing, and public accommodations. Completing a hiring-tool audit does not resolve all discrimination duties.
laws.timing: Existing law; separate from the 2023 start of Local Law 144 enforcement.
laws.appliesTo: Covered employers, employment agencies, housing providers, and public accommodations within the City Human Rights Law’s jurisdiction.
obligations: Avoid prohibited discrimination, including covered disparate-impact practices under §8-107(17).
Meet applicable reasonable-accommodation duties. Protected characteristics and coverage extend beyond the hiring audit’s minimum categories.
laws.enforcement: NYC Commission on Human Rights enforcement and civil actions under §8-502, subject to procedural and election-of-remedies rules.
laws.limits: A general civil-rights law, not an AI-specific audit mandate. Coverage, protected grounds, defenses, and exceptions depend on the activity. AI relevance is an application of these general duties.

laws.title: State Human Rights Law — discrimination safeguards
laws.description: Statewide discrimination protections remain relevant to AI-assisted hiring, housing, and other covered decisions, including decisions affecting people in NYC.
laws.timing: Existing statewide law; a separate framework from NYC Local Law 144.
laws.appliesTo: Covered employers, employment agencies, housing providers, and other regulated actors under the State Human Rights Law.
obligations: Avoid prohibited discrimination and comply with applicable accommodation duties.
Assess discriminatory effects in employment under §296(5-b), including job-relatedness, business necessity, and less discriminatory alternatives.
laws.enforcement: The New York State Division of Human Rights administers the law. Follow its guidance on complaints and available remedies.
laws.limits: This is a general civil-rights law, not a statewide version of NYC’s AEDT audit rule. AI relevance is an application of technology-neutral duties; coverage and exceptions require separate analysis.

laws.title: Synthetic performers in advertising
laws.description: Commercial advertisers with actual knowledge of a synthetic performer in their advertisement must conspicuously disclose its use.
laws.timing: Signed 11 December 2025; operative 180 days after enactment. In force by this review.
laws.appliesTo: Businesses producing or creating commercial advertisements for property or services. A synthetic performer is a human-like digital asset not recognizable as an identifiable natural performer.
obligations: Include a conspicuous disclosure in the covered advertisement when the advertiser actually knows it uses a synthetic performer.
laws.enforcement: The statute specifies $1,000 for a first violation and $5,000 for subsequent violations.
laws.limits: Exclusions cover audio ads, AI used solely for language translation, qualifying promotion of expressive works, and advertising media that merely publish or distribute the ad.

codeSections.detail: Synthetic performer means a human-like digital asset not recognizable as an identifiable natural performer.
Actual-knowledge disclosure duty and specified civil penalties.
Expressive-work promotion, audio, translation and publishing-media exclusions.

practicalSteps: Ask advertising suppliers whether performers are synthetic and preserve the response with the approved creative.
For a real person’s likeness or voice, separately review consent and digital-replica rights; an AI label does not replace them.

laws.title: Fashion Workers Act — digital replica consent
laws.description: Model management businesses and clients have specific consent duties before creating or using models’ digital replicas.
laws.timing: Core duties began 19 June 2025. Registration requirements began 21 December 2025.

sources.label: Department of Labor: scope and effective dates

laws.appliesTo: Covered model management companies, model management groups, and clients working with models in New York.
obligations: A model management company must obtain separate written consent for creation or use of the model’s digital replica, specifying purpose, scope, pay and duration.
Management companies may not create, alter or manipulate an AI digital replica without the model’s clear, conspicuous and separate written consent.
Clients must obtain clear, conspicuous prior written consent covering the replica’s scope, purpose, pay and duration.
laws.enforcement: Department of Labor complaints and enforcement under §1038; the provision authorizes $3,000 for an initial violation and $5,000 for a subsequent violation. Other statutory remedies and procedures also apply.
laws.limits: Replica consent is only part of the Fashion Workers Act. Model management registration, compensation and workplace duties remain relevant; a general services or representation agreement is not automatically adequate replica permission.

codeSections.detail: Separate management-company consent and required details.
Restriction on AI creation, alteration or manipulation without consent.

practicalSteps: Keep replica permissions separate from general representation terms, and compare each proposed reuse with the approved purpose and duration.
Identify whether the purchaser, agency and other intermediaries each have duties; do not assume one party’s release resolves all requirements.

laws.title: Deceased performers’ digital replicas
laws.description: New York’s post-mortem publicity law includes remedies for specified unauthorized uses of deceased performers’ digital replicas.
laws.timing: Current codified text includes December 2025 amendments. Rights are time-limited and subject to statutory conditions.
laws.appliesTo: Covered deceased personalities and performers domiciled in New York at death, and holders of their statutory rights.
obligations: Obtain the relevant right holder’s consent for covered replica uses in audiovisual works, sound recordings, or live musical performances.
laws.enforcement: Civil claims can recover statutory or compensatory damages, attributable profits, and potentially punitive damages.
laws.limits: Knowledge, authorization, domicile, duration, and other conditions matter. Exceptions protect specified parody, criticism, news, biographical, and other expressive uses. This is not a blanket ban on synthetic media.

laws.title: Nonconsensual sexually explicit synthetic media
laws.description: A depicted person can bring a civil claim over the unauthorized disclosure or publication of covered sexually explicit, digitally manipulated material.
laws.timing: Current statutory text reviewed 22 September 2026; filing periods depend on publication and discovery.
laws.appliesTo: Publishers or distributors who know or reasonably should know that the depicted individual did not consent to the relevant creation or dissemination.
obligations: Obtain knowing, voluntary consent in a signed plain-language agreement meeting the statute’s requirements.
A disclaimer that the individual did not participate does not by itself provide a defense.
laws.enforcement: Available civil remedies include injunctions, compensatory and punitive damages, and reasonable costs and attorney fees.
laws.limits: The law includes protected-expression, public-interest, and legal-proceeding exceptions. This entry concerns the synthetic-media provision; New York has two sections numbered 52-c.

laws.title: Personalized algorithmic pricing disclosures
laws.description: Covered offers of prices determined by algorithms using a consumer’s personal data must carry a clear disclosure alongside the price.
laws.timing: Disclosure law took effect 10 November 2025, according to the attorney general’s implementation notice.
laws.appliesTo: Entities doing business in New York that advertise or offer covered personalized algorithmic prices to New York consumers.
obligations: Display the statutory notice that the price was set by an algorithm using the consumer’s personal data, clearly and contemporaneously with the price.
laws.enforcement: The attorney general must first send a cease-and-desist notice with a cure timeline. Continued violations can lead to injunctions and penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.
laws.limits: Not all dynamic pricing qualifies. Exceptions include specified insurance and financial entities and some existing-subscriber discounts; a narrow transport-fare exclusion also applies.

laws.title: Manipulated media in political communications
laws.description: Political communications using materially deceptive media require disclosure when the distributor or publisher actually knows the material is deceptive.
laws.timing: 2024 measure, with subsequent amendments reflected in the current statute.
laws.appliesTo: Persons and organizations distributing covered political communications with realistic, materially altered or fabricated media.
obligations: Use the prescribed manipulation disclosure in a legible visual format or in audible notices.
Audio notices appear at the beginning and end, and at intervals of no more than two minutes for longer audio.
laws.enforcement: An affected candidate can seek expedited injunctive relief and reasonable court costs and attorney fees under the statutory conditions.
laws.limits: Exceptions include satire or parody, qualifying news reporting, and specified broadcasters or initial third-party dissemination. Other campaign disclosure obligations still apply.

laws.title: Public inventory of state-agency AI
laws.description: The Office of Information Technology Services maintains an inventory of state-agency AI systems that may directly affect the public.
laws.timing: 2025 framework; inventory publication is annual, on 30 December.
laws.appliesTo: State agencies using covered AI systems that materially influence public safety, welfare, or rights.
obligations: Submit required information at least 60 days before annual publication, including the systems’ purposes and uses.
ITS publishes the inventory on the state open-data website and submits it to specified state leaders.
laws.enforcement: Statutory agency reporting duties administered by ITS.
laws.limits: Security-sensitive or legally exempt information can be withheld. Basic calculations and specified rule-based automation are excluded. This is not a general private-business AI audit mandate.

laws.title: Government automated-employment tool disclosures
laws.description: State agencies publish annual lists of covered automated employment tools. A separate provision addresses local public bodies and education entities to the extent feasible.
laws.timing: Annual 30 December disclosure cycle. Temporary §402-a is scheduled to be repealed 1 July 2028.
laws.appliesTo: State agencies; separately, counties, cities, towns, villages, school districts, and other listed public or educational bodies. Definitions exclude the legislature and judiciary from state agencies.
obligations: List the tools, describe them, identify when use began, and summarize their purposes and uses.
The separate covered-entity disclosure duty operates to the extent feasible under §402-a.
laws.enforcement: Statutory public-body reporting obligations; this is separate from NYC’s private-employer bias-audit regime.
laws.limits: Covered employment uses extend beyond hiring to matters such as wages, discipline, promotion, and termination. Check the different definitions and scheduled 2028 changes.

laws.title: SHIELD Act — security of private information
laws.description: The SHIELD Act requires reasonable security for covered private information about New York residents, including information used in AI prompts, storage or retrieval systems.
laws.timing: Security requirements are in force. Breach-notification duties are separately listed under GBL §899-aa.
laws.appliesTo: Any person or business owning or licensing computerized data containing a New York resident’s statutory private information. Coverage is not limited to businesses physically located in New York.
obligations: Maintain reasonable administrative, technical and physical safeguards, including secure disposal.

Use the statutory security-program route or qualify as a compliant regulated entity; the program route includes staff coordination and training, risk assessment, vendor safeguards by contract, testing and appropriate disposal.
laws.enforcement: Attorney general enforcement under §899-bb(2)(d). This section does not create its own private right of action.
laws.limits: Small businesses receive a proportionate safeguards standard, not a blanket exemption. The definition uses fewer than 50 employees OR under $3 million annual gross revenue in each of the last three fiscal years OR under $5 million year-end assets. Private information is defined by §899-aa.

codeSections.detail: Covered data, including qualifying biometrics and medical/insurance information.

practicalSteps: Inventory the private information that enters prompts, embeddings, logs and uploaded files.
Review vendor retention, training use, access controls and deletion terms; document your security assessment.

laws.title: Fair business practices & AI product claims
laws.bill: General Business Law §349 · FAIR Business Practices Act
laws.description: New York’s current business-practices law prohibits unfair, deceptive, and abusive conduct. AI marketing and sales promises should be assessed under this general framework.
laws.timing: Current amended §349 checked 30 September 2026, including the 2026 chapter amendment.
laws.appliesTo: Covered commercial conduct with New York connections; the statute expressly addresses certain out-of-state businesses and New York businesses serving people elsewhere.
obligations: Avoid misleading AI claims and material omissions. Assess unfairness and abuse under the statutory standards.
laws.enforcement: Attorney general enforcement can include injunctive relief and restitution. Section 349(h) provides a private remedy for deceptive acts, with its own requirements.
laws.limits: This is not an AI-specific evaluation mandate. Keeping evidence for performance and safety claims is a practical application of the general law.

laws.title: Consumer subscriptions, trials & cancellation
laws.description: Automatic-renewal and continuous-service offers require clear terms, affirmative consent, acknowledgment, and accessible cancellation.
laws.timing: Current requirements in force; codified text checked 30 September 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Businesses making covered offers to New York consumers buying for personal, family, or household purposes.
obligations: Disclose price, billing frequency, renewal, and cancellation terms before consent; provide a retainable acknowledgment.
Offer simple cancellation through the same medium as signup, without obstruction.
Apply the required notices for qualifying trials, renewals, and material changes; price increases have additional conditions.
laws.limits: Consumer definitions, offer duration, sector exceptions, and transaction details matter. Do not apply this summary automatically to every B2B contract.

laws.title: New York Child Data Protection Act
laws.description: Restricts processing and sale of covered minors’ personal data, with age-specific consent and necessary-processing rules.
laws.timing: Effective 20 June 2025. This law is already operative; it is separate from the upcoming SAFE for Kids Act.
laws.appliesTo: Operators controlling processing of covered users’ personal data from online services, apps or connected devices, and their processors. A covered user is in New York and actually known to be under 18, or uses a service primarily directed to minors; the definition is broader than identified account holders.
obligations: For users 12 or younger, processing must meet the statutory COPPA standard. For ages 13–17, processing must be strictly necessary for a listed purpose or supported by the required informed consent.

Separate optional consent from other transactions, make refusal prominent and withdrawal easy, and observe restrictions on repeated requests. Do not purchase or sell covered data, subject to the statutory third-party protections.
Within 30 days of learning the user is covered, delete impermissibly processed data and direct processors to do so; notify relevant third-party operators.
Use binding processor terms addressing instructions, deletion/return, assistance, compliance assessments and onward processors.
laws.limits: Necessary internal operations expressly exclude marketing, advertising and research/development. A general acceptance of terms is not the required optional consent. Do not assume minors’ prompts may be reused to train a model just because the service needs to process them to answer.
laws.enforcement: The attorney general may seek injunctions, restitution, disgorgement including destruction of unlawfully obtained data, damages and penalties up to $5,000 per violation under §899-mm.

codeSections.detail: Covered users, personal data, operator and processor definitions.
Sale/purchase restriction, deletion and downstream notices.
Binding processor contracts and deletion evidence.

practicalSteps: Map separately the use of prompts to deliver a response, retention of chat history and reuse for model improvement.
Check vendor contracts and deletion workflows against the covered-minor data actually shared.

laws.title: Safe by Design Act — platform safeguards for minors
laws.description: Adds age assurance, protective defaults, and parental controls for covered platforms, including integrated AI companions.
laws.timing: Effective 1 January 2027.
laws.appliesTo: Platforms used by covered New York minors with public/semi-public profiles, private messaging, and specified social-media or gaming/transaction features; see the full definition.
obligations: Conduct required age assurance before making the specified interaction features or an integrated AI companion available. The statutory fallback does not permit self-declared age alone.
Apply privacy defaults restricting specified access and interactions by unconnected adults, and the restrictions on recommending minors’ profiles.
Disable integrated AI companions by default for covered minors. A parent’s override must be separate from other settings and follow the prescribed notice process.
Assess the separate parental-connection and spending-control requirements for covered games and younger users.
laws.enforcement: Attorney general enforcement under §1547 includes injunctions, restitution, disgorgement, damages and civil penalties up to $5,000 per violation after the effective date.
laws.limits: The platform definition combines several features; it does not capture every website or standalone chatbot. Fiction-only game characters have a defined exclusion. Article 45-B parental permission does not displace separate restrictions in the new Article 48 minors law.

codeSections.detail: AI companion, integration and covered-platform tests.
Age assurance, privacy defaults and parental settings.
Age assurance and default disabling of integrated companions.

practicalSteps: Inventory public profiles, messaging, feed/game features and companion integration against the platform definition.
Design separate parental controls and review companion access against all overlapping statutes before launch.

laws.title: SAFE for Kids Act — feeds & overnight notifications
laws.description: Restricts covered addictive social feeds and overnight feed notifications for minors without the required parental consent.
laws.timing: Effective 25 January 2027; final implementing rules are published at 13 NYCRR Part 700.
laws.appliesTo: Covered operators of addictive social media platforms serving covered users in New York. The law and rules define the feed, platform, and age-assurance tests.
obligations: Before providing a covered addictive feed, establish adult status through a permitted age-assurance method or obtain the required parental consent for a covered minor.
Do not send covered addictive-feed notifications between midnight and 6 a.m. Eastern without the required consent. Feed and nighttime-notification consents must be separately controllable.
Meet the final rules’ age-assurance, appeals and data-use protections; the age-status appeal process requires a response or information request within 10 business days.
Do not degrade ordinary access or raise prices because a user lacks permission for an addictive feed, except as necessary for compliance.
laws.limits: Not every recommendation engine or platform is covered. Check statutory feed exclusions, the final rules’ platform tests and exemptions, and the distinction between this feed law, child-data restrictions and companion laws.

sources.label: Attorney general: final rules and commencement

laws.enforcement: Section 1508 authorizes attorney general remedies, including penalties up to $5,000 per violation, subject to its separate 180-day enforcement timing. Adoption, operative duties and the enforcement timetable should not be conflated.

codeSections.detail: No discriminatory reduction in ordinary access for lack of feed permission.
Final implementation rules: consent, age methods, appeals and data safeguards.
Attorney general remedies and separate enforcement timing.

practicalSteps: Separate feed selection from general content access, and design independent consent switches for feeds and nighttime alerts.
Retain evidence of age-method testing and route age-status appeals to an accountable reviewer.

laws.title: Living-person likeness & voice consent
laws.description: Separate from AI disclosure rules, New York protects a living person’s identity against specified unauthorized advertising or trade uses.
laws.timing: Existing statutory protection; current §51 checked 30 September 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Covered uses in New York of a person’s name, portrait, picture, likeness, or voice for advertising or trade.
obligations: Obtain the required prior written consent for covered uses; assess exceptions and the permitted scope of each release.
laws.enforcement: Section 51 authorizes injunctions and damages, including potential exemplary damages for knowing violations.
laws.limits: This is not a ban on every reference or expressive use. A synthetic-performer disclosure does not replace permission to use a real person’s identity.

laws.title: Lawyers: professional duties when using AI
laws.description: Lawyers remain responsible for the quality, confidentiality and accuracy of AI-assisted work. These professional rules govern the lawyer’s conduct.
laws.timing: Existing professional rules. Court-hosted compilation amended through 1 July 2026 checked for this entry.
laws.appliesTo: Lawyers and law firms subject to the New York Rules of Professional Conduct, including practice in NYC.
obligations: Provide competent and diligent representation; meet client-communication and fee duties.
Protect confidential information and make reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access, disclosure or use.
Meet tribunal candor duties, including correction of knowingly false material statements; supervise lawyers and nonlawyer work as required.
laws.enforcement: Violations of the binding rules can lead to attorney discipline.
laws.limits: The Rules are binding; accompanying bar-association comments are explanatory, not separately enacted rules. Court-specific filing requirements and client terms require separate checks. These rules do not create a universal requirement to disclose every use of AI.

sources.label: Court-hosted July 2026 Rules compilation · comments distinguished

practicalSteps: Open and verify every cited authority and material factual statement before relying on an AI draft.
Check a tool’s retention and training settings before entering client material; record authorization and safeguards.
Set review responsibility and billing rules for AI-assisted work.

laws.title: Licensed professionals: confidentiality and scope of practice
laws.description: Covered licensed professionals must protect client information and stay within their authorized and competent practice. These existing rules matter when AI is used for professional work.
laws.timing: Existing regulation; official indexed text checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Covered Title VIII professions, including accountancy, engineering, architecture, psychology, and social work; profession-specific exceptions and additional rules apply.
obligations: Do not disclose personally identifiable information obtained professionally without prior client or patient consent, unless authorized or required by law.
Observe limits on competence, authorized practice, and delegation.
laws.enforcement: The regulation defines conduct that can support professional disciplinary proceedings.
laws.limits: This is not an AI-specific rule or a rule for every consultant. Lawyers have separate court rules; medicine has a separate disciplinary framework. Review the provisions for the actual license.

codeSections.detail: Confidentiality of personally identifiable professional information.

practicalSteps: Check the rules for your particular license before sending client or patient information to an AI service.
Use an appropriately qualified reviewer for professional conclusions; a tool’s output does not extend your licensed scope.

laws.title: Recording conversations and AI meeting notes
laws.description: AI recording tools operate within existing eavesdropping law. New York generally permits a participant to record their own conversation, but this does not resolve other states’ laws or professional confidentiality duties.
laws.timing: Existing statute; definitions and offense checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: People using tools to record or intercept covered communications; the participants’ locations and method of recording matter.
obligations: Avoid unlawful wiretapping, mechanical overhearing and interception/access to electronic communications under the statutory definitions.
laws.enforcement: Unlawful eavesdropping under §250.05 is a class E felony.
laws.limits: This is not blanket permission to deploy a meeting bot. Other participants’ jurisdictions, confidentiality duties, court rules and contract terms can add restrictions. The consent tests vary with the type of communication.

codeSections.detail: Definitions and the relevant sender/receiver or party consent tests.
Unlawful eavesdropping is a class E felony.

practicalSteps: Identify participants’ locations and obtain clear agreement before enabling recording or transcription.
Set who can access the transcript, where it is stored and when it is deleted.

laws.title: School records: student data privacy
laws.description: School use of AI must fit existing protections for covered student and staff records. Tool approval and permitted data use are separate questions.
laws.timing: Existing requirements. Statutory contractor duties and NYSED implementation materials checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Covered educational agencies and contractors receiving student records or specified teacher/principal evaluation data.
obligations: Include the parents’ bill of rights and required contract-specific information when a contractor receives covered data.
Contractors must limit access and use to authorized services, provide safeguards and encryption, and comply with disclosure and breach-reporting requirements.
Apply the relevant Part 121 data-security plan and contractor rules alongside the statute.
laws.enforcement: NYSED’s chief privacy officer oversees the statutory process; sanctions and remedies depend on the violation.
laws.limits: Coverage follows the statutory schools, data and contractor definitions. NYSED does not certify a list of compliant products. A general product-training purpose should not be assumed to be an authorized school service.

sources.label: NYSED · contractor contracts and scope FAQ

codeSections.detail: Covered schools/data, parents’ rights and contract disclosures.
Contract data-security plans and contractor controls; NYSED explains the framework.

practicalSteps: Check whether student work, names, assessments or teacher/principal records will reach the AI vendor.
Agree the permitted use, subcontractors, security and exit/deletion arrangements before deployment; do not assume a free tool is outside the rules.

laws.title: Financial services: cybersecurity and AI risks
laws.description: Covered financial-services entities must operate risk-based cybersecurity programs. DFS explains how existing requirements address AI use and AI-enabled threats.
laws.timing: Part 500 remains in force. The final two-year transition for the 2023 amendments ended 1 November 2025.
laws.appliesTo: Persons operating, or required to operate, under covered New York Banking, Insurance or Financial Services Law authorizations; §500.19 sets full and limited exemptions.
obligations: Document risk assessments and update them at least annually and when business/technology changes materially alter cyber risk.
Apply third-party security policies, access protections and other required controls, subject to the actual exemption.
Report defined cybersecurity incidents to DFS promptly and within 72 hours of determination; submit the annual compliance certification or acknowledgment by April 15.
laws.enforcement: DFS examination and enforcement under applicable law.
laws.limits: Not every AI vendor is itself DFS-regulated, and not every cyber event meets the incident definition. Limited exemptions retain duties. Guidance explaining AI risks is distinct from the binding regulation.

codeSections.detail: Covered entities, cybersecurity incidents and exemptions.
Risk assessments and third-party service-provider security.

practicalSteps: Include AI vendors and access to nonpublic information in the third-party risk review.
Check the actual exemption before selecting controls and record who handles the DFS incident deadline.

laws.title: NYC subscription cancellation: Click to Cancel
laws.description: Covered consumer subscriptions need clear terms and accessible cancellation. This can matter when selling or subscribing to an AI service.
laws.timing: Effective 1 October 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Covered automatic-renewal and continuous-service offers to consumers within NYC’s jurisdiction.
obligations: Provide cancellation through all offered consent channels; in-person signups also need an online option.
Do not obstruct or unreasonably delay cancellation. Follow applicable disclosure and notice rules.
laws.enforcement: DCWP civil penalties and restitution provisions.
laws.limits: Section 5-110.3 exempts specified financial entities, franchise services, alarm operators, and service-contract businesses. State law also needs review.

sources.label: Adopted city rule · text and exemptions
NYC · consumer guidance and complaint route

laws.title: Data breaches involving AI tools or vendors
laws.description: Unauthorized access to covered private information can trigger notice duties even without proof that data was downloaded.
laws.timing: In force; current codified text includes the 30-day notice limit and expanded private-information definition.
laws.appliesTo: Owners or licensees of computerized private information about New York residents; data holders acting for others have separate notice duties.
obligations: Notify affected residents as quickly as possible without unreasonable delay, within 30 days after discovery, subject to the law-enforcement delay rule.
Data holders must notify the owner/licensee immediately and within 30 days. Required resident notices also trigger notices to the AG, Department of State, State Police and DFS.
Follow the statutory content and delivery rules; document any applicable inadvertent-disclosure/no-harm determination.
laws.enforcement: The attorney general can seek statutory remedies and penalties under §899-aa(6).
laws.limits: Not every mistaken AI output is a data breach. The defined data and unauthorized-access/acquisition tests matter. The narrow no-harm exception requires written records; other sector notice obligations may also apply.

codeSections.detail: Resident/owner notices, 30-day limits and law-enforcement delay.
Delivery, notice content and agency notifications.

practicalSteps: Create a vendor incident contact and escalation process before uploading personal records.
If an incident occurs, preserve discovery dates and access logs and assess whose information was exposed; do not wait for certainty of misuse.

laws.title: Employee electronic-monitoring notices
laws.bill: Civil Rights Law §52-c (electronic monitoring; Senate lists §52-c*2)
laws.description: AI tools monitoring employee email, calls or internet use can fall within New York’s existing electronic-monitoring notice law.
laws.timing: In force; covered employees must receive prior written notice upon hiring and an accessible workplace notice.
laws.appliesTo: Private employers with a New York place of business that monitor the specified employee communications or internet use. State and political-subdivision employers are excluded.
obligations: Give covered new hires written or electronic notice and obtain written or electronic acknowledgment.
Post the electronic-monitoring notice conspicuously where affected employees can view it.
laws.enforcement: Attorney general enforcement; maximum civil penalties of $500 for a first offense, $1,000 for a second and $3,000 for later offenses.
laws.limits: The narrow maintenance/protection exception requires non-individualized monitoring solely for system maintenance or protection. Notice is not permission to ignore other privacy or discrimination laws. New York has two sections numbered 52-c; this entry links the monitoring provision.
practicalSteps: Check whether an AI productivity or security tool captures communications or individual internet activity.
Add the required notice and acknowledgment to onboarding, and retain evidence of the workplace posting.

laws.title: Employee identifiers and public AI outputs
laws.description: Existing restrictions on exposing employee identifiers are relevant when HR material is placed in public AI outputs or unrestricted files.
laws.timing: Existing law; current text checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Employers handling the employee information specified in §203-d.
obligations: Do not publicly disclose employee Social Security numbers, display them on identification/time cards or put them in unrestricted files unless otherwise required by law.
Do not communicate covered employee identifiers to the general public; listed items include home contacts, personal email, login/password information and driver’s-license numbers.
laws.enforcement: The labor commissioner may impose up to $500 for a knowing violation; missing safeguard policies can be presumptive evidence of knowledge.
laws.limits: This is a public-disclosure and identifier rule, not a categorical ban on every vendor transfer. SHIELD, monitoring, confidentiality and contract duties need separate review.
practicalSteps: Remove identifiers before publishing AI-generated HR examples or sharing a public chat link.
Limit access to HR source files and check outputs for personal identifiers.

laws.title: Hiring and employees’ personal accounts
laws.description: Employers cannot evade personal-account access protections by using an AI screening service to request the same credentials or private content.
laws.timing: In force since March 2024.
laws.appliesTo: Covered public and private employers and their agents, employees and applicants; specified law-enforcement, fire and corrections agencies are excluded.
obligations: Do not request, require or coerce personal-account credentials, access in the employer’s presence, or reproduction of content obtained by those prohibited means.
Do not penalize an employee or refuse to hire an applicant for refusing the prohibited disclosure.
laws.enforcement: The statute prohibits the access demands and related retaliation; §201-i(4) supplies a defense for action taken to comply with legal requirements.
laws.limits: Business accounts, employer systems, certain device access and legally required screening have qualified exceptions. Publicly available information is treated differently. An employer-paid device does not automatically authorize access to personal accounts.

codeSections.detail: Legal-compliance defense, exceptions and excluded agencies.

practicalSteps: Review the data sources and permissions requested by any social-media screening vendor.
Keep private-account credentials and forced logins out of the recruiting workflow.

laws.title: AI screening, consumer reports and adverse decisions
laws.description: AI-generated background or eligibility reports may fall within New York’s Fair Credit Reporting Act when the statutory reporting-agency and report definitions are met.
laws.timing: In force; current §§380-a and 380-b include the April 2026 credit-history amendments.
laws.appliesTo: Consumer reporting agencies and report users in covered credit, insurance, employment, housing and other transactions. A report can concern character or personal characteristics, not only a credit score.
obligations: Obtain reports only for permitted purposes and give the application-stage notice required by §380-b.
Apply §380-b(d)’s restriction on employment use of consumer credit history and its specific exceptions.

For the credit, insurance and housing adverse actions described in §380-i, notify the consumer, identify the agency and explain the right to obtain the report. Reporting agencies must reinvestigate qualifying disputes under §380-f.
laws.enforcement: Sections 380-l and 380-m provide civil liability for willful and negligent noncompliance, subject to the applicable requirements.
laws.limits: Not every internal AI ranking is a consumer report. Federal FCRA obligations, including employment procedures, require separate analysis; the listed §380-i adverse-action categories do not themselves describe the full federal employment process.

codeSections.detail: Permitted purposes, notice and employment credit-history restrictions.
Disputes and correction of unverified or incorrect information.
Specified adverse-action notices and report-sharing limits.

practicalSteps: Ask a screening vendor whether it supplies consumer reports and document the intended permissible purpose.
Provide a way to identify the report behind a decision and direct people to the reporting agency’s dispute process.

laws.title: Unsafe AI companion features for minors
laws.bill: Chapter 368 of 2026 · S9051B · new GBL Article 48, §§1800–1805
laws.type: Enacted state statute; commencement requires confirmation
laws.description: Restricts unsafe AI companion features for minors and requires age checks before offering those features.
laws.timing: Signed 28 October 2026; not yet operative. Commencement is not reconciled: the final bill text says 1 January 2027, while the sponsor’s signing update reports a chaptered change to 1 June 2027.
laws.appliesTo: Operators offering covered conversational generative AI to users in New York; coverage is broader than relationship-focused companions.
obligations: Restrict listed unsafe features unless permitted adult status is established.
Follow age-assurance alternatives and data-use limits.
laws.enforcement: Final B text provides attorney general penalties up to $25,000 per violation, without the earlier draft’s express private action.
laws.limits: Customer-service and research-assistance exceptions require responses confined to that purpose; internal-business uses are separately addressed. Confirm commencement against the chapter amendment.

codeSections.detail: Restrictions, exceptions, remedies and age assurance.

practicalSteps: Check actual product behavior and age controls against the final commencement documents.

Sponsor’s signing update: reported June commencement

laws.title: Digital-replica clauses in services contracts
laws.description: Certain contract clauses substituting a digital replica for a person’s work are unenforceable when the statute’s combined conditions are met.
laws.timing: Applies to contracts entered into or modified on or after 1 January 2025.
laws.appliesTo: Personal or professional services agreements authorizing a digital simulation of an individual’s voice or likeness in place of work they otherwise would perform.
obligations: Assess the specificity of the intended use and the counsel or labor-organization protections in §5-302(1)(c) before relying on a replica clause.
laws.enforcement: The qualifying provision is void and unenforceable as to a new digitally replicated performance.
laws.limits: All statutory conditions matter, including the exception for uses consistent with the contract and the fundamental character of the recorded work. Other contract provisions remain unaffected; this is not a blanket ban on digital replicas.

codeSections.detail: Combined conditions making a replica provision unenforceable.
Remaining contract provisions and the replica definition.

practicalSteps: Have the person and their representative review the specific replica use before signature; retain the separately signed terms where applicable.

name: Connecticut

laws.title: Connecticut Data Privacy Act: data and consequential AI decisions
laws.description: The amended privacy law broadens coverage and gives consumers rights concerning personal data and automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.
laws.timing: Core law effective 1 July 2023; major coverage and rights changes took effect 1 July 2026, with further P.A. 26-64 changes effective 1 October 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Since July 2026, coverage includes businesses in or targeting Connecticut processing at least 35,000 consumers in the prior year, persons processing consumers’ sensitive data, or persons offering their data for sale. Payment-only exclusions and statutory exemptions apply.
obligations: Honor applicable access, correction, deletion, portability, sale and advertising opt-outs, and opt-outs from qualifying consequential automated profiling.
Provide the applicable information and avenues to question consequential profiling; the current text contains additional rights concerning reasons, data used and specified housing decisions.
Maintain data minimization and security, obtain required sensitive-data consent, and perform assessments for covered heightened-risk processing.
laws.enforcement: Exclusive Attorney General enforcement; no private right of action under the CTDPA. Ordinarily respond to consumer requests within 45 days, with a permitted extension in qualifying circumstances.
laws.limits: The consumer definition excludes employment and commercial contexts. Section 42-517 contains entity and data exemptions. Sensitive-data and sale coverage mean a small consumer count does not by itself establish exemption.
practicalSteps: Check sensitive-data and sale activity as well as consumer volume.
Map consequential decision tools to notices, request handling, opt-outs and assessment records.

laws.title: AI employment decision disclosures
laws.description: Enacted prospective rules require specified vendors and employers to explain covered AI technology used as a substantial factor in employment decisions.
laws.timing: Sections took effect 1 October 2026, but the duties address covered technology deployed on or after 1 October 2027. They are upcoming operational requirements as of this review.
laws.appliesTo: Deployers using AI that materially influences covered hiring, promotion, discipline, discharge, training or employment terms, and specified vendors of technology marketed or configured for those decisions.
obligations: For covered deployments from 1 October 2027, give the required plain-language interaction disclosure unless AI interaction is obvious.
Before a covered employment decision, provide written information on the AI’s use, purpose, trade name, data categories and sources, and deployer contact details.
Covered vendors must supply information needed for deployer compliance; contractual allocation and trade-secret provisions have statutory conditions.
laws.enforcement: Attorney General enforcement; these sections do not create a private cause of action. A discretionary 60-day cure process is available for violations occurring on or before 31 December 2027.
laws.limits: General-purpose tools used incidentally and without material influence are excluded. The definition also excludes specified scheduling, planning, productivity-monitoring and workplace-safety uses. Existing discrimination and privacy rules may apply independently before 2027.

codeSections.detail: Defines covered employment decisions and substantial-factor technology.
Vendor information and deployer interaction/decision notices, tied to 2027 deployments.

practicalSteps: Identify which decision tools could materially influence employment outcomes.
Request the vendor information needed to prepare notices before the operational start date.

laws.title: AI companion disclosures and safeguards
laws.description: Enacted prospective rules address AI companions designed to sustain humanlike relationships, including disclosures, crisis safeguards and additional protections for minors.
laws.timing: Effective 1 January 2027; upcoming as of this review.
laws.appliesTo: Operators offering covered AI companions for personal use by individuals physically in Connecticut. Defined exclusions cover specified narrow business, educational, game, assistant and clinical uses.
obligations: From January 2027, implement and publish the required self-harm and violence-risk protocol, including appropriate resource or referral responses.
Prevent claims that a companion is human. Where a reasonable person could mistake it for a person, provide the prescribed continuing or periodic AI notice.
Where the operator knows or has reason to believe a user is under 18, apply the statute’s additional safety, interaction and parental-control requirements.
laws.enforcement: Attorney General enforcement under the enacted provisions; the companion sections do not create a general private action.
laws.limits: Not every chatbot is an AI companion. Narrow customer-service tools and other listed exclusions must meet their definitions; an upstream model supplier is not automatically the operator. The minor-specific rules are more detailed than this summary.

codeSections.detail: Defines AI companion, operator and excluded tools.
Crisis protocols, human-impersonation controls and AI notices.
Additional duties for known or reasonably known minors.

practicalSteps: Assess whether relationship-building features bring a product within the companion definition.
Prepare notice timing, crisis-response protocols and youth controls before January 2027.

laws.title: Notice of electronic workplace monitoring
laws.description: Connecticut’s existing electronic-monitoring law can matter when AI analyzes workplace communications or activity through covered monitoring equipment.
laws.timing: Existing law amended effective 1 October 2026; the additional new-hire statement applies to employees hired on or after that date.
laws.appliesTo: Employers collecting covered information about employee activities or communications on the employer’s premises through electronic equipment, subject to the statutory definition and exceptions.
obligations: Before covered monitoring, give notice of its types and specific workplace locations; conspicuous posting, including at the monitored locations, constitutes the required notice.
Before work starts, give employees hired from 1 October 2026 a plain-language written statement identifying prohibited activities that may be monitored without prior notice.
laws.enforcement: The Labor Commissioner may levy civil penalties: up to $500 for a first violation, $1,000 for a second and $3,000 for a third or subsequent violation.
laws.limits: Public-common-area security monitoring is excluded. Misconduct and criminal investigations have exceptions. Location disclosure has airport and reasonable security/employee-safety exceptions. The premises-based definition does not resolve every remote-work scenario.

codeSections.detail: Defines electronic monitoring and its limits.
Monitoring types, locations, posted notices and new-hire statements.

practicalSteps: Match notices and monitored locations to the actual AI-assisted monitoring.
Add the required plain-language statement to onboarding before an employee starts work.

summary: Current data-privacy and workplace-monitoring rules, plus separately dated upcoming AI employment and companion requirements.

name: Delaware

laws.title: Personal Data Privacy Act — duties through 2026
laws.description: Consumer privacy duties can apply to AI inputs and profiles. Until 2027, the profiling opt-out is specifically for solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.
laws.timing: Core law effective 1 January 2025; sale/targeted-advertising preference signals from 1 January 2026. Separate enacted amendments take effect 1 January 2027.
laws.appliesTo: Businesses operating in or targeting Delaware that processed at least 35,000 consumers in the prior year, excluding payment-only data, or 10,000 plus over 20% of revenue from data sales. Commercial/employment contexts and specified entities/data are excluded.
obligations: Provide consumer rights, notices and qualifying profiling opt-outs; support required preference signals.
Obtain required sensitive-data consent and use appropriate security.
The current assessment duty has its own 100,000-consumer threshold and covers heightened-risk activities created/generated from 1 July 2025.
laws.enforcement: Delaware DOJ enforces; no private action under this chapter. Cure opportunities have been discretionary since 1 January 2026.
laws.limits: Do not confuse the main coverage threshold with the assessment threshold. A separate entry explains the 2027 amendments.
practicalSteps: Count Delaware consumers separately from payment-only records.
Identify which AI decisions are solely automated and significant.

laws.title: 2027 privacy amendments: wider coverage and AI impact assessments
laws.description: Enacted amendments lower coverage thresholds and add more explicit requirements for consequential profiling and data recipients. These provisions are future duties, not the current 2026 rules.
laws.timing: Effective 1 January 2027.
laws.appliesTo: Coverage expands to 10,000 consumers (excluding payment-only data), or 5,000 plus over 20% revenue from data sales, and specified third parties. The assessment provision uses a separate 50,000-consumer threshold.
obligations: At the assessment threshold, document regular impact assessments for profiling supporting automated decisions with significant effects, including inputs, outputs, metrics, limitations and safeguards.
Covered third-party recipients must follow required contracts and provide information supporting assessments.
Expanded access rights include inferences and whether data is processed for consequential profiling.
laws.enforcement: Delaware DOJ enforcement under §12D-111; the chapter does not create a private action.
laws.limits: Use the versions marked effective 1 January 2027. Exemptions remain relevant and this entry summarizes selected amendments, not every change.
practicalSteps: Recalculate coverage before January 2027.
Ask profiling vendors for data categories, evaluation metrics and post-deployment safeguards.

laws.title: Employee monitoring notices for AI-assisted workplace tools
laws.description: AI analysis of employee email, calls or Internet activity can fall within existing monitoring-notice requirements.
laws.timing: Existing statute; current code checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Employers with a Delaware place of business, including public employers, monitoring covered activity of Delaware employees.
obligations: Before covered monitoring, provide either an acknowledged one-time written/electronic notice or an electronic notice at least once each day the employee accesses employer-provided email/Internet services.
laws.enforcement: A violation carries a $100 civil penalty; a claim may be filed in a court with jurisdiction. Other available remedies are preserved.
laws.limits: A narrow exception applies to untargeted processes performed solely for system maintenance/protection. Notice does not override other privacy or discrimination duties.

codeSections.detail: Penalty, other remedies and maintenance exception

practicalSteps: Identify whether an AI productivity or security tool monitors individual communications or Internet activity.
Keep the acknowledgement with the policy version it covered.

laws.title: Data security and breach notification
laws.description: Reasonable security and breach-notice duties can cover personal information used by AI systems, including qualifying biometric authentication data.
laws.timing: Existing law; current code checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Persons conducting Delaware business and owning, licensing or maintaining defined personal information; notification duties differ for owners and custodians.
obligations: Maintain reasonable protection against unauthorized acquisition, use or disclosure.
Notify affected residents without unreasonable delay and generally within 60 days after determining a qualifying breach, subject to statutory exceptions.
Notify the AG when more than 500 residents require notice; qualifying Social Security number breaches require one year of free credit monitoring.
laws.enforcement: The Attorney General may seek relief and direct economic damages under §12B-104; other rights are preserved.
laws.limits: An appropriate investigation may establish that harm is unlikely. Encryption, compromised keys and regulator-specific provisions matter.
practicalSteps: Inventory biometric templates, credentials and identifiers held by AI suppliers.
Agree how the vendor will immediately report an incident to the data owner.

summary: AI-related privacy, workplace monitoring and security duties, with the enacted 2027 privacy changes shown separately from current requirements.

name: Florida

laws.title: Generative AI in political advertising
laws.description: Specified political communications using generative AI to depict a real person doing something that did not occur require an AI disclaimer.
laws.timing: Effective 1 July 2024.
laws.appliesTo: Covered political advertisements and electioneering communications with intent to injure a candidate or deceive about a ballot issue.
obligations: Include the statutory AI disclaimer in addition to other election disclaimers.
Meet format rules: print minimum 12-point bold; video visible throughout at least 4% of picture height; audio at least 3 seconds. Internet/graphic requirements also apply.
laws.enforcement: The Florida Elections Commission accepts complaints; failure to disclose can carry civil and criminal penalties.
laws.limits: Not a labeling mandate for every use of AI in political work; the depiction and intent conditions must be met.
practicalSteps: Review the exact disclaimer text in the statute before releasing creative.
Check every format and channel, including audio and mobile graphics.

laws.title: Digital Bill of Rights: profiling, sensitive data and consumer requests
laws.description: Covered consumers can access, correct or delete data and opt out of significant-decision profiling. Covered businesses also have vendor-contract and risk-assessment duties. A separate sensitive-data sale rule has broader coverage.
laws.timing: Core framework effective 1 July 2024.
laws.appliesTo: Main controllers generally need more than $1 billion in global annual gross revenue plus a qualifying online-advertising, smart-speaker/virtual-assistant or large app-store business model; controlled/controlling entities also matter. Section 501.715 separately reaches qualifying for-profit Florida businesses collecting consumer data without the billion-dollar threshold.
obligations: Honor authenticated access, correction, deletion and portability requests, plus opt-outs for sale, targeted advertising, consequential profiling, sensitive data and voice/facial-recognition data (§501.705).

Respond without undue delay and within 45 days; a justified extension adds at most 15 days with timely notice. Explain refusals and provide an appeal process; appeal decisions are due within 60 days (§§501.706–501.707).

Use processor contracts covering instructions, purpose, data types, duration, confidentiality, deletion/return, assessments and subcontractors. Processors must support requests, security and assessments (§501.712).

Document assessments for targeted advertising, data sales, sensitive data and specified risky profiling or other heightened-risk processing. Weigh benefits against risks and safeguards; §501.713 applies to activities generated on or after 1 July 2023.

Check §501.715 separately: qualifying businesses selling sensitive data need prior consent or the specified child authorization and must display the statutory sale notice, even outside the main controller threshold.
laws.enforcement: Department of Legal Affairs enforcement; up to $50,000 per violation, with specified enhancements. The law creates no private action.
laws.limits: The main consumer framework excludes employment/commercial contexts and has significant entity/data exemptions (§§501.703–501.704). It is not a right to reject every AI tool or a guarantee of human review. The assessment activity date is separate from the framework’s July 2024 commencement; small size alone does not resolve §501.715.

codeSections.detail: Consumer definition and narrow main-controller threshold.
Applicability and exemptions; check before relying on a right or duty.
Privacy rights, profiling opt-out and limits on inactive-device surveillance.
Processor assistance and required contract terms.
Public enforcement; no private action under this part.

practicalSteps: For a consumer request, identify the right you are exercising, keep the submission date and use the appeal route if refused.
For an AI deployment, document the coverage analysis, actual data uses and vendor roles before choosing safeguards.
Make a deletion or opt-out request reach relevant AI processors; do not assume a general vendor privacy policy supplies the required contract.

laws.title: Data security and breach reporting
laws.description: AI vendors and users handling covered personal information can face security and breach duties without the Digital Bill of Rights’ revenue threshold.
laws.timing: Existing law; the current 2026 code includes security, notification and disposal duties.
laws.appliesTo: Commercial covered entities and contracted processors; governmental entities have specified duties.
obligations: Use reasonable security measures and secure disposal.
Affected-person notice is generally due within 30 days after determining or having reason to believe a breach occurred.
Notify Legal Affairs within 30 days for 500 or more affected Florida individuals; processors generally notify their customer within 10 days.
laws.enforcement: Department of Legal Affairs enforcement; no private cause of action under this section.
laws.limits: Protected data includes specified identifiers, medical information, biometric data, geolocation and account credentials. Statutory exceptions, documented no-harm determinations and permitted delays require separate assessment.
practicalSteps: Assign incident ownership before sending personal information to an AI provider.
Require rapid vendor incident escalation and track the applicable notice clocks.

laws.title: AI meeting assistants and recording consent
laws.description: AI recording and transcription must fit Florida’s existing interception law. For ordinary consensual recording of covered communications, the statute requires prior consent from all parties.
laws.timing: Existing law.
laws.appliesTo: People intercepting covered wire, oral or electronic communications. Oral-communication coverage depends on a justified expectation against interception.
obligations: Obtain all-party prior consent when relying on §934.03(2)(d).
Do not unlawfully intercept, use or disclose covered communications.
laws.enforcement: Section 934.03 provides criminal penalties; additional remedies may apply under Chapter 934.
laws.limits: There are specific statutory exceptions. This is not a universal rule that every public conversation is protected, nor does Florida consent settle other jurisdictions or confidentiality duties.
practicalSteps: Confirm participant locations and consent before enabling an AI notetaker.
Offer a meeting option without recording and review transcript access and retention.

laws.title: Sexual deepfakes: prohibited conduct and removal requests
laws.description: Florida prohibits specified nonconsensual altered sexual depictions and requires covered platforms to provide a removal process. The rules address creation as well as distribution.
laws.timing: In force. Covered platforms had to establish their notice-and-removal process by 31 December 2025; the current code includes 2026 amendments.
laws.appliesTo: People engaging in the defined conduct involving realistic altered sexual images of an identifiable person, and websites/apps meeting the covered-platform definition. Florida jurisdiction includes an offense element or resulting harm occurring in the state.
obligations: Do not willfully generate a qualifying nonconsensual depiction. Solicitation and malicious promotion/possession have their own knowledge and intent elements (§836.13(2)–(4)).
Covered platforms must publish a clear, accessible process for signed removal requests identifying the content, nonconsent and contact details (§836.13(8)(a)–(c)).
After a valid request, remove the depiction as soon as possible and within 48 hours; make reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies (§836.13(8)(d)).
laws.enforcement: Specified conduct is a third-degree felony. A person harmed by conduct under subsection (2) or (4) may seek an injunction, the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, and fees/costs. Failure reasonably to comply with platform-removal duties invokes consumer-protection remedies.
laws.limits: Not every synthetic image is covered. The statute distinguishes conduct and platform duties and includes intermediary, reporting, law-enforcement and legal-proceeding exceptions. An AI disclaimer is not a criminal defense. Subsection (8) has its own platform exclusions; check both (8) and (9).

codeSections.detail: Definitions and separate creation, solicitation and promotion offenses.
Request contents, platform process and 48-hour removal deadline.

practicalSteps: If seeking removal, preserve the URL and evidence and submit a signed request through the platform’s stated process; keep a timestamp and acknowledgment.
If operating a covered service, assign someone to receive requests and handle the 48-hour deadline and duplicate-content search.
