laws.title: AI advertising and a person’s name or likeness
laws.description: Existing Florida consent requirements can matter when AI-generated advertising uses an identifiable real person’s name, portrait, photograph or likeness. The statute is broader than AI use.
laws.timing: Existing law; current 2026 statutory text checked. This entry does not treat proposed AI-specific amendments as enacted.
laws.appliesTo: Public use of a natural person’s name or likeness for trade, commercial or advertising purposes, subject to the statutory exceptions. The text also addresses minors and deceased people.
obligations: Obtain the required express written or oral consent from the person or the authorized rights holder before a covered commercial use (§540.08(1)).
For a minor, consent must come from a parent or guardian; for a deceased person, check who can authorize the use under the statute (§540.08(1)(c), (6)).
laws.enforcement: A qualifying claimant may seek an injunction and damages, including a reasonable royalty and punitive/exemplary damages. Unauthorized use of a covered armed-forces member’s likeness can also attract a civil penalty of up to $1,000 per violation.
laws.limits: Bona fide non-advertising news, certain authorized resales and incidental unnamed crowd photographs have exceptions. The statutory post-death limit is 40 years. It does not expressly create a general AI-labeling rule or settle every voice-cloning question; applying it to a particular AI depiction requires analysis.

codeSections.detail: Consent and authority to give it.

practicalSteps: Keep a record of permission covering the specific campaign and proposed synthetic alteration; written permission helps document an otherwise oral authorization.
If challenging an unauthorized advertisement, preserve the advert, where it appeared and the claimed endorsement.

laws.title: Lawyers: competence, confidentiality and AI-assisted work
laws.description: Professional duties continue when lawyers use AI. Rule comments expressly discuss generative AI, while the rule text supplies the binding obligations.
laws.timing: Existing rules; official Chapter 4 compilation dated 22 October 2026 checked.
laws.appliesTo: Florida Bar members and other lawyers authorized to practice in Florida.
obligations: Provide competent representation and comply with candor duties to tribunals.
Protect representation information, obtain required informed consent for disclosure, and take reasonable steps against unauthorized access.
Avoid illegal, prohibited or clearly excessive fees; exercise applicable supervision over nonlawyer assistance.
laws.enforcement: Violations can lead to professional discipline; a rule violation does not itself create a civil cause of action.
laws.limits: Comments guide interpretation and do not add duties. Ethics Opinion 24-1 is advisory, not binding, and is included only as supporting AI-specific guidance.

codeSections.detail: Competence; AI discussed in the comment.

practicalSteps: Verify AI-generated authorities and analysis before relying on them.
Review vendor retention, training and access terms before uploading client material; record the billing basis.

laws.title: Court filings: verify cited authorities, including AI output
laws.bill: Fla. R. Gen. Prac. & Jud. Admin. 2.515(d)(2) · AOSC26-12
laws.description: Signing a Florida state-court filing represents that its cited legal authorities exist and are accurately cited. This applies to lawyers and people representing themselves.
laws.timing: Amended rule and accompanying statewide order effective 15 June 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Signers of documents filed in Florida state courts, whether or not AI helped prepare them.
obligations: Read the filing and make the representations required by Rule 2.515(d)(2), including that cited authorities exist and are accurately cited.
laws.enforcement: After notice and an opportunity to be heard, a court may impose sanctions including reprimand, striking the document, dismissal, costs or attorneys’ fees.
laws.limits: This is a filing representation, not a general ban on AI or a separate AI-disclosure certificate. AOSC26-12 bars additional circuit-level AI disclosure/certification requirements for filings. Federal courts have their own rules.

sources.label: Adopted Rule 2.515 · appendix and effective date

codeSections.detail: Representations made on filing; authority verification.
Uniform statewide approach to AI filing certifications.

practicalSteps: Open each cited authority in a reliable source; check quotations, citations and what the authority actually supports.
Give self-represented users of drafting tools a verification step before filing.

laws.title: Patient records and AI scribes or document tools
laws.description: Existing medical-record duties matter when AI tools receive, summarize or store patient information.
laws.timing: Existing statute; 2026 codified text checked.
laws.appliesTo: Defined health-care records owners and custodians. Chapter 395 licensed facilities are excluded from this section.
obligations: Use written patient authorization for disclosure unless a statutory exception applies.
Maintain confidentiality/security policies and train employees.
Record third-party disclosures and their purpose; subsection (11) restricts onward disclosure.
laws.enforcement: Licensing authorities discipline licensees. The Attorney General may seek injunctions and fines up to $5,000 per violation against otherwise unlicensed records owners.
laws.limits: Definitions and disclosure exceptions control. This is not an AI-specific prohibition; HIPAA and other applicable law require separate analysis.
practicalSteps: Map what an AI scribe sends to the vendor, where it is retained and whether it is reused for training.
Check the applicable disclosure authority before enabling the tool.

laws.title: AI product claims and deceptive business practices
laws.description: Florida’s general unfair-and-deceptive-practices law can apply to marketing or selling AI products and services. Claims about accuracy, capabilities or safeguards need to be assessed under this existing standard.
laws.timing: Existing law; selected provisions checked against the 2026 statutes.
laws.appliesTo: Trade or commerce broadly includes advertising, offering and providing goods or services, including nonprofit activity. Section 501.212 excludes specified regulated persons or activities and other listed matters; this law does not use the Digital Bill of Rights’ billion-dollar threshold.
obligations: Do not engage in unfair, deceptive or unconscionable commercial practices or unfair methods of competition (§501.204).
laws.enforcement: State attorneys and the Department of Legal Affairs have enforcement powers, including injunctions and consumer-damages actions. Section 501.211 permits qualifying private declaratory/injunctive relief and actual-damages claims, with statutory conditions for fees and costs.
laws.limits: These sections do not create a universal AI-labeling or audit requirement. An incorrect AI output alone does not prove liability. Insurance, banking and other exclusions in §501.212 require checking; personal-injury claims are outside this part.

codeSections.detail: Excluded acts, claims and regulated activities

practicalSteps: Keep evidence supporting advertised AI capabilities, and review generated sales copy before publishing.
If challenging a service, preserve the advertisement, terms, receipts and relevant outputs; identify the misleading promise and resulting loss.

laws.title: AI-assisted hiring and employment discrimination
laws.description: Existing civil-rights protections matter when AI screens applicants, ranks workers or supports employment decisions. The statute governs prohibited discrimination, rather than prescribing a particular AI system.
laws.timing: Existing law; selected provisions checked against the 2026 statutes.
laws.appliesTo: The statutory employer definition generally requires 15 or more employees for each working day in at least 20 calendar weeks in the current or preceding year, and includes agents. Employment agencies, labor organizations and specified other actors have separately defined duties.
obligations: Do not unlawfully discriminate in hiring, discharge, compensation, employment terms or classifications because of a protected characteristic.
Employment advertisements must not express prohibited preferences; retaliation for opposing or participating in a proceeding concerning unlawful practices is prohibited.
laws.enforcement: A complaint to the Florida Commission on Human Relations generally must be filed within 365 days of the alleged violation. Administrative relief or civil litigation is subject to §760.11’s procedural requirements, with remedies depending on the route and findings.
laws.limits: Protected grounds include race, color, religion, sex, pregnancy, national origin, age, disability (the statute uses “handicap”) and marital status. Statutory qualifications, religious-organization exceptions and other coverage conditions matter. This entry does not establish a universal bias-audit duty or summarize subsection (8)’s separate workplace-training provisions.

codeSections.detail: Qualifications, exceptions and required workplace notice

practicalSteps: Review the criteria and outputs used by a screening vendor against lawful job requirements; keep a route for identifying and correcting discriminatory decisions.
Applicants can preserve the job advert, application, assessment instructions and decision correspondence. Check filing deadlines promptly; other laws can use different deadlines.

laws.title: Tenant screening, housing advertisements and AI
laws.description: AI-assisted tenant selection and housing advertisements remain subject to Florida’s Fair Housing Act where its coverage and conditions are met.
laws.timing: Existing law; selected provisions checked against the 2026 statutes.
laws.appliesTo: Covered dwelling sales, rentals, related services and advertising. Section 760.29 contains conditional exemptions, including specified private-owner, owner-occupied and other arrangements; exemption analysis differs by provision.
obligations: Do not deny housing or discriminate in covered terms or services because of race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status or religion.
Do not publish housing advertising expressing prohibited preferences or limitations (§760.23(3)).
Make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services where necessary to afford a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling (§760.23(9)(b)).
laws.enforcement: The Florida Commission on Human Relations accepts housing complaints, generally within one year. Section 760.35 provides a separate civil-action route with a two-year filing limit, procedural restrictions, and potential equitable relief, damages and fees.
laws.limits: This is not a blanket ban on automated screening or a statutory right to inspect every model. Ownership exemptions have conditions; do not assume a small landlord is exempt from every advertising rule. This entry covers housing, not all real-estate lending requirements.

sources.label: FCHR housing complaint route and timing

practicalSteps: Check tenant-screening criteria and AI-written advertisements for prohibited preferences; build a way to consider accommodation requests.
If affected, save the listing, screening communications, denial and accommodation correspondence, and check the relevant complaint route.

laws.title: Government AI work and public-records duties
laws.description: Records made or received in official business can fall within Florida’s public-records law regardless of their format. Applying that definition to prompts, outputs and vendor-held files requires examining their function and content.
laws.timing: Existing law; selected provisions checked against the 2026 statutes.
laws.appliesTo: State and local agencies, and entities acting on their behalf, within §119.011(2). Contractor duties in §119.0701 apply to a services contractor acting on behalf of the public agency; merely selling software does not automatically establish that status.
obligations: Preserve covered records and follow applicable retention and disposal schedules (§119.021).
Allow access to nonexempt public records; respond promptly and in good faith, redact validly exempt portions and identify the legal basis for withholding (§119.07).

Covered services contracts must address record maintenance, access, protected information and completion/transfer arrangements; electronic records must be supplied in a compatible format when the agency requests them (§119.0701).
laws.enforcement: Chapter 119 allows enforcement proceedings and includes penalties for violations. Covered contractors can face contractual enforcement and, where statutory conditions are met, production proceedings and enforcement costs under §119.0701.
laws.limits: Not every AI interaction is automatically a public record, and not every public record is publicly disclosable. Confidentiality, trade-secret and security exemptions need separate review. Retention periods depend on the applicable record series; this entry does not impose one universal period for AI chats.

codeSections.detail: Agency coverage and format-neutral public-record definition
Access, prompt response and withholding explanations
Contract scope, records clauses and enforcement

practicalSteps: Decide which AI work products document official business, and configure retention/export with the agency’s records custodian before enabling auto-deletion.
People researching government AI can request existing procurement contracts, policies or decision records from the agency; exemptions may require redaction.

summary: Florida rules relevant to everyday and professional AI use: privacy requests, recording, lawyer and court-filing duties, patient records, hiring, housing, advertising, deepfakes and government records. Open each entry for its scope, code sections and practical steps.

laws.description: An AI-specific consumer rule addresses misleading human impersonation by chatbots and other computer technology in trade or commerce.

laws.enforcement: A violation is a violation of the Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act; its enforcement and remedy conditions apply.

laws.description: Maine’s general prohibition on unfair or deceptive commerce can be relevant to unsupported claims about an AI service, its accuracy, or its human oversight.
laws.timing: Existing consumer-protection law; not a newly enacted AI-specific rule.
laws.appliesTo: Trade or commerce in Maine, subject to the Act’s scope and exceptions; the private consumer remedy has additional purchase and loss conditions.
obligations: Avoid unfair or deceptive commercial practices, including misleading representations about what an AI product or service does.
laws.enforcement: The Attorney General may seek injunctions and other statutory relief. Section 213 permits qualifying consumers with monetary or property loss to seek relief; a damages demand ordinarily precedes suit by 30 days.

Addresses qualifying consumer loss and pre-suit demand.

laws.title: Personal-data breach notification
laws.description: An AI vendor incident can trigger Maine’s existing breach-notification law when protected computerized personal information is acquired or misused within the statutory conditions.
laws.timing: Existing law in force; reviewed against the current codified provisions.
laws.appliesTo: Information brokers and other persons maintaining covered computerized personal information. Section 1347 defines the protected identifiers and breach.
obligations: Investigate a discovered breach promptly and reasonably to assess the likelihood of misuse.
Give required resident notice promptly and without unreasonable delay, generally within 30 days after becoming aware of the breach and identifying its scope; lawful investigative delays can apply.

A maintainer that does not own the information must immediately notify the owner when unauthorized acquisition is known or reasonably believed. Give required regulator notice and, for more than 1,000 notified persons, consumer-reporting-agency notice.
laws.enforcement: The Department of Professional and Financial Regulation enforces for persons it regulates; the Attorney General enforces for others. Statutory civil penalties and equitable relief are available.
laws.limits: The notice trigger differs for information brokers and other persons: for non-brokers, misuse must have occurred or be reasonably possible. Not every prompt, log, or security incident contains the defined personal information.

codeSections.detail: Defines breach and covered personal information.
Sets investigation, owner notice, resident notice and timing.
Addresses reporting agencies and regulator notice.
Provides enforcement and qualifying equivalent-procedure provisions.

practicalSteps: Map which AI vendors receive covered identifiers.
Set a vendor incident escalation route that leaves time to investigate and meet notification deadlines.

laws.title: Nonconsensual intimate images, including digital fabrications
laws.description: Massachusetts criminalizes qualifying harmful distribution of intimate visual material, including digitally created or altered depictions that appear authentic.
laws.timing: Relevant 2024 amendments took effect 18 September 2024.
laws.appliesTo: A person knowingly distributing covered visual material of an identifiable person, where the harm, intent or recklessness, consent and privacy conditions are met.

laws.enforcement: Criminal penalties apply; the statute preserves other available remedies, including equitable relief.

Sets distribution, harm, mental-state and consent conditions.

Apply the required computer controls, including access security and specified encryption measures to the extent technically feasible.

codeSections.detail: Defines personal information and owning or licensing it.
Written security program and ongoing safeguards.

Check AI vendor contracts, access controls, retention and security practices against the security program.

obligations: Avoid unfair or deceptive commercial acts, including misleading statements about characteristics, benefits, sponsorship, approval or quality.
laws.enforcement: Section 358-A:10 authorizes an action by a person injured by a violation, with statutory remedies and enhanced damages for a knowing or willful violation.
laws.limits: AI examples are practical applications of a general statute. Liability requires the statutory elements; an inaccurate AI output alone does not establish a claim.

name: New Jersey

laws.title: Consumer data privacy and consequential profiling
laws.description: Covered AI processing is subject to consumer rights, purpose limits, sensitive-data protections and risk assessments. The general law does not cover residents acting in an employment or commercial context.
laws.timing: Core law effective 15 January 2025; universal sale/targeted-advertising opt-outs required from 15 July 2025. The sensitive-data sale amendment took effect 30 June 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Controllers doing business in NJ or targeting its residents that process at least 100,000 consumers in a calendar year (excluding payment-only data), or at least 25,000 and derive revenue or a discount from personal-data sales. Specified entities/data are exempt. The 2026 sensitive-data sale restriction expressly reaches below these volume thresholds.
obligations: Provide privacy notices and access, correction, deletion, portability and opt-out mechanisms; covered consequential profiling has an opt-out right (§166.10).
Respond to verified requests within 45 days, subject to the statutory extension; provide an appeal route (§166.7).
Obtain required sensitive-data consent, minimize collection and document heightened-risk assessments; do not sell sensitive data under the 2026 amendment (§166.12).
laws.enforcement: Attorney General has exclusive enforcement; this privacy law creates no private action. The initial mandatory cure period has expired (§§166.17, 166.19).
laws.limits: A profiling opt-out is not a ban on every recommendation. Check the definition of significant decisions, data exemptions and separate discrimination duties.
practicalSteps: Map model inputs, inferred profiles and vendor disclosures to the notice and permitted purposes.
Test that an opt-out prevents the covered processing throughout the AI workflow.

laws.title: Data brokers, data collectors and sensitive-data sales
laws.description: New duties can affect AI training-data businesses and services selling or licensing consumer datasets. The statute distinguishes brokers without a direct consumer relationship from collectors selling to brokers.
laws.timing: Approved and generally effective 30 June 2026. The Division’s public-registry provision is inoperative for 270 days after enactment; that delay is limited to §2(b).
laws.appliesTo: Defined brokers and collectors selling or licensing New Jersey consumers’ personal data, subject to detailed statutory exclusions. A consumer must act in an individual or household context.
obligations: Annually register, pay the applicable fee and submit required business/data-practice information under §166.20(c)–(d).
Do not sell or license sensitive data unless a specified statutory exclusion applies (§166.22).
laws.enforcement: The Division may pursue registration/information penalties; §166.23 sets a $50,000-per-record civil penalty for specified sensitive-data sales or licensing violations.
laws.limits: Registry implementation and registration procedure require checking Division instructions. The 270-day delay does not postpone the entire act. Processor disclosures and listed sector/data exclusions require separate analysis.

codeSections.detail: Immediate effect and narrow registry delay

practicalSteps: Check how a dataset was acquired and whether customers have a direct relationship with each data supplier.
Separate sensitive data from datasets offered for sale or licensing; confirm exclusions before release.

laws.title: Customer information breaches, including AI-vendor exposure
laws.description: Unauthorized access to covered customer information can trigger notice even when it occurs through an AI tool or its supplier. The incident law has a different scope from the consumer privacy act.
laws.timing: Existing breach-notification law; 2019 amendment includes qualifying online-account credentials.
laws.appliesTo: Businesses operating in NJ and public entities maintaining covered computerized customer records. The personal-information and breach definitions in §161 control.
obligations: Notify affected NJ customers as expediently as possible and without unreasonable delay, subject to investigation/restoration and authorized law-enforcement delay.
Report to the Division of State Police before customer disclosure. A data custodian must immediately alert the owner after discovery.
If concluding misuse is not reasonably possible, document that determination and retain it for five years.
laws.enforcement: Willful, knowing or reckless violations of the specified provisions are unlawful practices under the Consumer Fraud Act (§56:8-166).
laws.limits: Not every accidental AI upload satisfies the breach definition. Encryption, permitted access, misuse risk, credentials-only notices and statutory exceptions matter.
practicalSteps: Include AI suppliers in the incident-response contact list.
Record discovery, affected data categories and the basis for the notification decision.

laws.title: Law Against Discrimination and automated decisions
laws.description: The existing discrimination statute applies when automated tools affect employment, housing, public accommodations, credit or contracting. Buying a third-party tool does not by itself remove the user’s responsibility.
laws.timing: Existing statutory duties. The Attorney General and Division on Civil Rights explained their application to algorithms in January 2025.
laws.appliesTo: Entities and activities covered by the Law Against Discrimination, including employers, housing providers and public accommodations; coverage depends on the statutory category.
obligations: Do not discriminate on a protected basis in covered decisions, including decisions made or assisted by AI.
Address required disability accommodations; evaluate discriminatory outcomes as well as intentional treatment.
laws.enforcement: The Division on Civil Rights enforces the LAD; statutory claims and remedies depend on the facts and available forum.
laws.limits: The cited agency document explains existing law and creates no new obligations. It does not establish a universal AI audit or automatically decide that any particular model is unlawful.

codeSections.detail: Covered discriminatory practices; discussed in the official agency interpretation

practicalSteps: Ask a vendor for evidence about the tool’s relevant performance and limitations.
Review rejected applicants or customers for potentially discriminatory patterns and provide an accommodation route.

name: North Carolina

laws.title: Unfair and deceptive trade practices
laws.description: General unfair-trade rules can apply to misleading AI product claims, sales practices and services. They are not an AI-specific approval or certification regime.
laws.timing: Existing law.
laws.appliesTo: Business activities in or affecting commerce; the statute expressly excludes professional services rendered by members of a learned profession.
obligations: Do not use unfair or deceptive practices in covered commerce.
laws.enforcement: An injured person may sue under §75-16; assessed damages are trebled.
laws.limits: The professional-services exclusion is activity-specific; do not assume every business associated with a professional is exempt. The advertising-media exception also has conditions.
practicalSteps: Keep evidence supporting claims about AI accuracy, safety and capabilities.
Review sales copy and chatbot statements before publication.

laws.title: Personal information: breach notification
laws.description: AI-related data exposure can trigger existing breach-notification duties when the statutory personal-information and breach definitions are met.
laws.timing: Existing law; notification deadlines run from discovery or notification.
laws.appliesTo: Covered businesses owning/licensing personal information, and custodians maintaining others’ data.
obligations: Notify affected people without unreasonable delay, subject to permitted investigative and law-enforcement delays.
A custodian must notify the owner/licensee immediately after discovery.
Notify the Attorney General when consumer notice is given; more than 1,000 notices also trigger nationwide credit-reporting-agency notice.
laws.enforcement: Violation is treated as a §75-1.1 violation; an individual must suffer resulting injury to bring a private claim.
laws.limits: Not every prompt leak meets the definitions. Apply §75-61 and the special exclusions in §75-65(a); notice timing is not a fixed 30-day rule.

codeSections.detail: Definitions of protected information and security breach

practicalSteps: Identify data owners and escalation contacts before using an external AI vendor.
Keep an incident plan that separates owner, custodian and regulator notices.

laws.title: AI-generated intimate images: disclosure restrictions
laws.description: The private-image law expressly includes realistic depictions generated or modified using algorithms or AI.
laws.timing: Existing statute; AI-image language appears in the 2024 amendment.
laws.appliesTo: Knowingly disclosing identifiable intimate imagery with specified harmful intent, without affirmative consent, and with the required creation/privacy circumstances.
obligations: Do not disclose covered imagery where all §14-190.5A(b) elements are met.
laws.enforcement: Criminal penalties apply; affected people also have a civil action, including statutory damages and possible image-destruction relief.
laws.limits: Not a ban on all synthetic images. Statutory exceptions include specified public-interest uses and service providers hosting another person’s images. The civil filing period is limited.
practicalSteps: Do not treat an AI label as permission to publish intimate depictions.
Create a reporting and escalation route for suspected nonconsensual imagery.

laws.title: Intimate deepfakes and child protections
laws.description: Pennsylvania criminal provisions expressly reach specified AI-generated sexual depictions. Adult intimate-image and child-protection offenses have different elements.
laws.timing: Act 125 approved 29 October 2024; effective 60 days later.
laws.appliesTo: People engaging in the conduct defined by each offense, including specified dissemination and possession involving artificially generated material.
obligations: Section 3131(a)(2) prohibits disseminating a qualifying artificial sexual depiction with intent to harass, annoy or alarm another, subject to statutory defenses.
Section 6312 separately addresses knowing dissemination and intentional viewing/knowing possession of covered child sexual abuse material.

laws.title: Recording and AI transcription of conversations
laws.description: AI meeting bots and call-transcription tools can implicate Pennsylvania interception law. The ordinary consent exception requires prior consent from all parties.
laws.timing: Existing statute; current chapter checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Interception, use or disclosure of covered wire, electronic or oral communications. The definitions and the context of the communication matter.
obligations: For reliance on §5704(4), obtain every party’s prior consent before interception.
Do not use or disclose intercepted contents in violation of §5703.
laws.enforcement: Section 5703 provides criminal liability; §5725 provides a civil remedy for qualifying unlawful interception, disclosure or use.
laws.limits: Specific statutory exceptions exist. Interstate calls can involve other jurisdictions; a bot invitation or platform icon should not automatically be treated as sufficient consent.
practicalSteps: Use a clear pre-recording consent process and provide a non-recorded alternative.
Check where participants are located before activating transcription.

laws.title: Personal-information breach notification
laws.bill: Breach of Personal Information Notification Act §§2–5.4, 8; 73 P.S. §§2302–2305.4, 2308
laws.description: An AI or vendor incident involving defined personal information can trigger notification and additional credit-monitoring duties.
laws.timing: Existing law; Act 33 changes took effect 26 September 2024.
laws.appliesTo: Covered entities maintaining, storing or managing computerized personal information about Pennsylvania residents. Public agencies and contractors have additional deadlines.
obligations: Notify residents without unreasonable delay after determining a qualifying breach, subject to statutory allowances.
Notify the AG concurrently when more than 500 Pennsylvania individuals require notice; insurance-specific exceptions apply.
Apply §5.4’s credit-report and 12-month monitoring requirements where its notification and compromised-data conditions are met.
laws.enforcement: The Attorney General enforces the act as an unfair or deceptive practice (§8).
laws.limits: The definition requires unauthorized access/acquisition and the stated loss-or-injury condition. The general private-entity rule is not a universal fixed-day deadline; agency rules differ.
practicalSteps: Include prompt logs, document uploads and AI-vendor storage in the incident inventory.
Determine whether exposed credentials or identifiers meet the statutory definition before setting notices.

name: Rhode Island

laws.title: Synthetic media in election communications
laws.description: Rhode Island restricts qualifying deceptive synthetic media in election communications and provides a disclosure route and specified exceptions.
laws.timing: Effective 2 July 2025; the restriction applies within 90 days of the relevant election.
laws.appliesTo: Candidates, campaign and political committees, political parties, and persons or entities making independent expenditures, where the depicted candidate will appear on the ballot.
obligations: Do not distribute covered deceptive or fraudulent synthetic media when the statutory knowledge and election-period conditions apply, unless an exception is satisfied.
For the disclosure exception, identify AI generation or manipulation clearly; visual and audio formats have specific placement, size, duration and repetition requirements.
laws.enforcement: A depicted candidate may seek injunctive relief against distribution and statutory damages remedies in the circumstances described in § 17-30-2. The court may award fees to a prevailing party.
laws.limits: Exceptions include satire or parody and qualifying news coverage that clearly identifies inauthentic content. Broadcaster, cable and intermediary protections are conditional. The law does not cover every AI-created political statement.

codeSections.detail: Covered communications, 90-day period and disclosure formats.

practicalSteps: Check election dates, the depicted candidate and the distributor’s role before publishing synthetic campaign material.
Review the final audio or video itself to confirm required disclosures remain legible or audible.

laws.title: Consumer privacy, website notices and automated profiling
laws.description: The Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act provides data rights and controls for covered profiling, alongside a separate website transparency provision.
laws.timing: Effective 1 January 2026. The assessment duty applies to processing activities created after that date, as specified in § 6-48.1-7.
laws.appliesTo: Core controller duties apply to qualifying for-profit businesses targeting or operating in Rhode Island: at least 35,000 customers, excluding payment-only data, or at least 10,000 plus more than 20% of gross revenue from personal-data sales in the prior year.
obligations: Provide access, correction, deletion, portability and opt-outs for targeted advertising, sale, and solely automated profiling with legal or similarly significant effects.
Maintain reasonable security, obtain required sensitive-data consent, and document covered high-risk processing assessments and processor contracts.
Check § 6-48.1-3 separately for commercial website and online-service disclosure duties; do not assume the numerical thresholds answer that question.
laws.enforcement: Attorney General enforcement; the Act expressly creates no private right of action.
laws.limits: Entity and data exemptions, including specified employment-related data, must be checked. The right to opt out of consequential profiling does not cover every automated recommendation.

codeSections.detail: Consumer rights, including specified profiling opt-outs.

practicalSteps: Evaluate website transparency and core controller coverage separately.
Document which AI decisions significantly affect consumers and how a valid opt-out will be implemented.

laws.title: Security safeguards, vendors and breach notices
laws.description: Existing Rhode Island security and breach rules can apply to personal information held in AI systems, prompts, transcripts or vendor records.
laws.timing: Existing Identity Theft Protection Act requirements; current code includes separate public-agency notification timing.
laws.appliesTo: Covered persons and state or municipal agencies collecting, using, maintaining or otherwise handling the statute’s defined personal information of Rhode Island residents.
obligations: Maintain a risk-based security program and reasonable retention and secure-destruction practices.
Require appropriate safeguards in written agreements with nonaffiliated third parties handling the information.

For a qualifying breach presenting significant identity-theft risk, notify promptly: generally no later than 45 days for private persons or 30 days for public agencies after confirmation and ascertainment of the required notice information.
laws.enforcement: Attorney General enforcement under § 11-49.3-5; reckless and knowing or willful violations carry statutory civil penalties. Additional Attorney General and credit-reporting notices apply when more than 500 residents are notified.
laws.limits: The statutory personal-information definition and identity-theft-risk trigger control. Law-enforcement delay and qualifying alternative procedures may apply; this entry is not a complete incident-response checklist for public agencies.

codeSections.detail: Risk-based security, retention, destruction and vendor contracts.
Breach trigger, timing and lawful delay.
Civil penalties and Attorney General enforcement.

practicalSteps: Check whether AI vendors can meet the organization’s security and incident-notification arrangements.
Maintain a breach triage process that distinguishes private and public-agency deadlines.

laws.enforcement: Graduated criminal penalties apply; harmful intent or financial gain can trigger felony treatment.
laws.limits: Read the knowledge and reasonable-expectation-of-privacy elements and law-enforcement exception. The statute is specific to intimate imagery, not every AI replica.

codeSections.detail: Digital forgery, identity and effective-consent definitions

Escalate suspected intimate-image abuse promptly.

laws.title: Personal identifying information: breach notification

laws.appliesTo: Businesses operating in South Carolina that own/license covered data; separate duties apply to custodians.
obligations: Notify affected residents when the breach meets the illegal-use/material-risk-of-harm test.

laws.title: Consumer Data Protection Act and consequential profiling
laws.description: Covered consumers have rights over personal data and certain consequential profiling. AI deployment can also require sensitive-data consent, purpose limits and a documented assessment.
laws.timing: Core law effective 1 January 2023; current amended code checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Persons doing business in or targeting Virginia that process at least 100,000 consumers annually, or 25,000 plus over 50% gross revenue from data sales. Exemptions include specified government, financial, HIPAA, nonprofit and higher-education entities; employment-context data is excluded.
obligations: Provide access, correction, deletion, portability and qualifying profiling opt-outs; respond within 45 days, subject to one permitted extension (§577).
Minimize collection, obtain required sensitive-data consent, maintain security and provide privacy notices. Current §578 also prohibits selling or offering precise geolocation data.
Assess heightened-risk processing, including specified profiling; §580 also addresses services directed to known children.

laws.limits: This consumer statute is not a general workplace AI law. Coverage exemptions and the definition of significant effects must be checked.
practicalSteps: Identify which profiles influence significant consumer decisions.
Make deletion and opt-out requests reach downstream AI processors.

laws.title: Conversation recording and AI note-taking
laws.description: Virginia’s interception law includes a party-or-prior-consent exception relevant to AI recording and transcription.
laws.timing: Existing statute; current code checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: People intercepting, using or disclosing covered wire, electronic or oral communications; the communication definitions and circumstances matter.
obligations: To rely on §19.2-62(B)(2), the recorder must be a party or have prior consent from one party.
Do not unlawfully use or disclose intercepted communications.
laws.enforcement: Section 19.2-62(A) makes the specified unlawful interception, disclosure or use a Class 6 felony; other subsections address service-provider disclosure.
laws.limits: This exception does not settle another state’s law on an interstate call, confidentiality, privilege, employment policy or permission to upload content to an AI vendor.
practicalSteps: Tell participants when transcription is being used and check other jurisdictions.
Review the vendor’s retention and training settings before recording sensitive discussions.

laws.title: Breach notification for covered personal information
laws.description: An AI-system or supplier incident can trigger separate notification duties when it exposes the personal information and fraud risk defined in this statute.
laws.timing: Existing statute; current text checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Owners/licensees of computerized covered personal information of Virginia residents; custodians have separate owner-notification duties. Sector exclusions and special payroll rules apply.
obligations: When the statutory unauthorized-access/acquisition and identity-theft-or-fraud conditions are met, notify affected residents and the AG without unreasonable delay.
Provide the required incident description, affected data types, protective measures and assistance information.
laws.enforcement: The AG enforces the statute; specified financial institutions are overseen by their primary state regulator. Insurance-regulated entities have an exclusion.
laws.limits: There is no universal fixed-day limit in this section. Defined data combinations, encryption/redaction, fraud risk and authorized investigation delay control.
practicalSteps: Check whether prompts or uploaded files contain the listed identifier combinations.
Require the supplier to give facts needed for a timely fraud-risk and notice assessment.

laws.title: Maryland Online Data Privacy Act
laws.bill: Md. Code, Commercial Law §§14-4701 et seq.
laws.description: Covered AI uses must meet consumer-rights, minimization and risk-assessment duties. Sensitive-data processing follows a strict-necessity standard; consent alone is not the general test.
laws.timing: Effective 1 October 2025; current codification is Subtitle 47. The original act has a separate prospective-application provision dated 1 April 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Persons operating in or targeting Maryland that processed at least 35,000 consumers in the preceding year (excluding payment-only data), or at least 10,000 plus over 20% gross revenue from data sales. Entity/data exemptions and the individual/household consumer definition apply.
obligations: Provide rights including an opt-out from profiling supporting solely automated decisions with significant effects (§14-4705).
Limit sensitive-data processing to what is strictly necessary for the requested service; do not sell sensitive data (§14-4707).
Document regular assessments for heightened-risk processing, including each algorithm used (§14-4710); required processor contracts are addressed in §14-4708.
laws.enforcement: Consumer Protection Division enforcement; §14-4713 excludes the Consumer Protection Act’s private-action provision for a violation of this subtitle while preserving other remedies.
laws.limits: This is not a blanket right to opt out of all AI. Do not mistake original 2024 section numbers beginning 14-46 for the current 14-47 codification.
practicalSteps: Document why each sensitive input is strictly necessary for the requested product.
Assess the actual algorithms used, not only the vendor’s generic privacy policy.

laws.title: Facial recognition in employment interviews
laws.description: Employers need a specified signed waiver before using a facial-recognition service to create a facial template during an applicant’s interview.
laws.timing: Effective 1 October 2020.
laws.appliesTo: Employers using technology that analyzes facial features for recognition or persistent tracking to create a machine-interpretable facial template during an employment interview.
obligations: Obtain the applicant’s signed waiver before the covered use.
The plain-language waiver must give the applicant’s name, interview date, consent to facial recognition and whether the applicant read it.
laws.enforcement: Section 3-717 imposes the employer prohibition but does not state a separate penalty within that section.
laws.limits: This narrowly concerns facial-template creation during interviews. It is not a general authorization for video analytics, discrimination or unrelated biometric processing.
practicalSteps: Ask the interview-platform provider whether any facial template is created.
If it is, confirm consent before enabling the feature and preserve the signed waiver.

laws.title: Personal-information security and vendor breaches
laws.description: Existing security and incident rules apply to covered personal information handled by businesses and nonaffiliated service providers, including AI suppliers.
laws.timing: Existing statute; current provisions checked 3 November 2026.
laws.appliesTo: Businesses owning, maintaining or licensing defined personal information of Maryland residents; obligations differ between data owners/licensees and custodians.
obligations: Maintain reasonable security appropriate to the data and business; covered written service-provider contracts must require reasonable security.

Promptly investigate a breach and, unless misuse is reasonably unlikely, notify affected individuals as soon as practicable and within 45 days of discovery/notification, subject to statutory exceptions.
A custodian must notify the owner/licensee as soon as practicable and within 10 days. Notify the AG before required individual notices; retain a no-notice determination for three years.
laws.enforcement: These duties sit within Maryland’s Personal Information Protection Act; regulator-compliance provisions in §14-3507 may affect the analysis.
laws.limits: Definitions, regulatory safe harbors and law-enforcement delays matter. These requirements are separate from MODPA’s consumer-count thresholds.
practicalSteps: Check AI supplier contracts for security and prompt incident cooperation.
Keep an incident log that distinguishes vendor discovery from owner notification.
